---
title: "EIR, HBR, prevalence, and cases"
---




Transmission intensity enters MINTverse as an EIR or an HBR and leaves it as under-five
prevalence and clinical cases. Each of those four quantities is either a single number
describing the setting in the year the campaign lands or a path through time, and that
distinction decides which package produces it.

## The four quantities

The **entomological inoculation rate (EIR)** is infectious bites per person per year, and it
sets the force of infection in the transmission model the emulator stands in for. It is the
quantity `stateMINT` runs from. `estimint` infers it from a prevalence or from an HBR.

The **human biting rate (HBR)** is bites per person per year, infectious or not. It is the EIR
divided by the sporozoite rate, so the numbers are large, typically in the tens or hundreds of
thousands per year. `mosquito_delta` scales the mosquito density, and it reaches the
transmission model through the HBR.

Prevalence is reported throughout MINTverse as the under-five value on a 0 to 1 scale. It
appears both as an input (`prev_y9`, a single number describing the setting at the decision
point) and as an output (a 157-step trajectory from the emulator).

Cases are clinical malaria episodes, all-age, per 1000 population, and an emulator output only,
so nothing in the pipeline takes cases as an input and there is no cases-to-anything inversion
to run. They are floored at zero.

## Values and series

| Quantity | What it is | Units | Value or series | Produced by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| EIR | transmission intensity | infectious bites / person / year | single value | `estimint` |
| HBR | biting pressure | bites / person / year | single value | `estimint` |
| Prevalence | infected share, under-5 | proportion, 0–1 | input value **or** 157-step series | input or `stateMINT` |
| Cases | clinical episodes, all-age | per 1000 population | 157-step series | `stateMINT` |

`estimint` returns an equilibrium, the transmission intensity that a setting sustains at the
moment the decision is taken. It has no time axis and cannot acquire one, so it cannot say what
the EIR will be two years after a PBO campaign, only what it would be in a setting that had
already settled under one.

Only `stateMINT` returns a path. A trajectory, a comparison of trajectories, or an endline
value three years out has to come from the emulator.

::: {.callout-note}
## EIR and equilibrium

`estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta` returns two numbers, `eir_baseline` and `eir_new`. Both are
equilibria. `eir_new` is the intensity a setting would settle at with a different mosquito
density, not the EIR at some later date, so the two values do not bracket a trajectory between
them. Any transient between them is the emulator's business.
:::

## The time grid

Every trajectory the emulator returns is laid on one grid of 157 fortnightly steps, built
around the day the campaign lands. The simulations behind `stateMINT` run a six-year burn-in
first, letting the transmission model settle into equilibrium from arbitrary initial
conditions. That burn-in is **discarded** and never reaches the emulator.

What remains starts at day 2190, the start of year 6, and runs in 14-day windows. The first
three years are pre-campaign baseline, during which nothing changes. At day 3285, the start of
year 9, the campaign switches on. `dn0_future`, `itn_future`, `irs_future`, `lsm` and `routine`
are zero for every step before that day, and take their value from it onwards. Roughly three
years of response follow.

The grid is written into the artefact rather than hard-coded, so it can be read back.

::: {#957f10ea .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

artifact = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)
cfg = artifact.preprocessing_config

abs_t = cfg["model_start_day"] + cfg["window_size"] * np.arange(cfg["n_steps"])
years = (abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]) / 365
idx_y9 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"])))

print(f"steps                {cfg['n_steps']}")
print(f"window               {cfg['window_size']} days")
print(f"grid starts          day {abs_t[0]}")
print(f"campaign             day {cfg['intervention_day']} -> step {idx_y9} (day {abs_t[idx_y9]})")
print(f"grid ends            day {abs_t[-1]}")
print(f"years from campaign  {years[0]:+.2f} to {years[-1]:+.2f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
steps                157
window               14 days
grid starts          day 2190
campaign             day 3285 -> step 78 (day 3282)
grid ends            day 4374
years from campaign  -3.00 to +2.98
```
:::
:::


The name `prev_y9` is literal. It is the annual mean under-five prevalence in year 9, the year
the campaign lands. Passing a measured prevalence to `estimint` asserts that this is the
setting as it stands on the day the nets are distributed.

The three pre-campaign years serve as a sanity check. No campaign acts on them, so they show
the setting under the nets it already has, and a baseline that starts somewhere other than the
prevalence you supplied means the covariates do not describe the setting you think they do.
Plotting in `years` rather than raw days puts the campaign at zero, so scenarios line up on one
x-axis.

## See also

The net mix, the spraying coverage and the larval control that switch on at day 3285 are
described in [Interventions and nets](interventions.qmd), and the three estimators and the
emulator that consume them in [The models](models.qmd). Please see [Estimating EIR from
prevalence](../04-estimint/estimating-eir.qmd) for the inversion in practice.
